observatories.name: FAST (Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical Telescope)
observatories.description: A 500-metre single-dish radio telescope built in a natural depression in Guizhou, with an active surface of 4,500 metal panels that forms a movable parabolic shape. It observes radio wavelengths from 10 cm to 4.3 m.
highlights: Construction began in 2011 and first light came in September 2016; it was fully operational on 11 January 2020.
Its first discoveries were two pulsars, PSR J1859-01 and PSR J1931-02, in August 2017.
By November 2024 it had found over 1,000 pulsars.

observatories.name: Arecibo Observatory
observatories.description: Home of a 305-metre spherical reflector dish built in a natural sinkhole; the dish collapsed on 1 December 2020 and will not be rebuilt. The site is still an operating observatory with a 12-metre radio telescope for VLBI, a LIDAR facility and a visitor center.
highlights: Formally opened as the Arecibo Ionospheric Observatory on 1 November 1963.
Its dish was the world's largest single-aperture telescope for 53 years, until China's FAST surpassed it in 2016.
In 2022 the NSF announced the telescope would not be rebuilt; an educational facility, Arecibo C3, is to be established instead.
observatories.film: Arecibo appears in the film Contact (1997) as the dish used in the search for extraterrestrial signals.

observatories.name: Green Bank Telescope
observatories.description: A fully steerable radio telescope with a 100-metre-diameter collecting area, operated by the Green Bank Observatory. It works from meter to millimeter wavelengths (0.1-116 GHz).
highlights: Described as the world's largest fully steerable radio telescope.
It replaced the 300 Foot Radio Telescope, which collapsed in 1988 from structural failure.
About 85% of the local celestial hemisphere is accessible, and it is used for astronomy roughly 6,500 hours a year.

observatories.name: Effelsberg 100-m Radio Telescope
observatories.place: Effelsberg, Bad Münstereifel, Eifel (Ahr Hills), North Rhine-Westphalia
observatories.description: A fully steerable 100-metre radio telescope operated by the Max Planck Institute for Radio Astronomy. It observes pulsars, gas and dust clouds, star-forming regions, magnetic fields and jets from black holes.
highlights: Inaugurated on 12 May 1971 and in full operation in 1972.
For 29 years it was the largest fully steerable radio telescope on Earth, until the Green Bank Telescope in 2000.
It serves as a station in international radio-telescope arrays that produce the sharpest cosmic images.

observatories.name: Parkes radio telescope "Murriyang"
observatories.place: Parkes Observatory, near Parkes, New South Wales
observatories.description: CSIRO's 64-metre movable-dish radio telescope, named Murriyang in November 2020. It is nicknamed The Dish.
highlights: Built in 1961 and fully operational by 1963.
The 64 m dish was one of several antennas that received live television of the Apollo 11 Moon landing; NASA stayed with Parkes for the remainder of the 2.5-hour broadcast.
More than half of currently known pulsars were discovered at Parkes; the first fast radio burst was identified in Parkes archival data recorded in 2001.
observatories.film: Parkes is the dish in The Dish (2000), the story of how it relayed the Apollo 11 moonwalk television.

observatories.name: Lovell Telescope, Jodrell Bank Observatory
observatories.description: A 76.2-metre (250 ft) steerable radio telescope operated by the University of Manchester. Jodrell Bank is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
highlights: Completed in 1957; named after Sir Bernard Lovell in 1987 and Grade I listed in 1988.
It tracked Soviet and US space probes in the Space Race, receiving lunar imagery from Luna 9 in 1966.
It was influential in early detections of quasars, astrophysical masers and Einstein rings.

observatories.name: RATAN-600
observatories.description: A ring of 895 rectangular radio reflectors, each 2 m x 7.4 m, in a 576 m diameter circle at 970 m altitude, run by the Special Astrophysical Observatory. With its central receiver it has the resolving power of a nearly 600-metre dish.
highlights: Began operation in 1977.
Described as the world's largest-diameter individual radio telescope.
Used to study blazars and other radio sources.

observatories.name: Nobeyama 45 m radio telescope
observatories.place: Nobeyama Radio Observatory, near Minamimaki, Nagano
observatories.description: A 45-metre millimetre-wave radio telescope at 1,350 m altitude, part of the National Astronomical Observatory of Japan. It operates across 1-80 GHz and studies star formation and galaxy evolution.
highlights: Built in 1982 with positioning errors under 0.1 mm.
NAOJ credits it with advancing Japanese radio astronomy to world-class standards.
It has operated for over 40 years.

observatories.name: Allen Telescope Array
observatories.place: Hat Creek Radio Observatory, Shasta County, California
observatories.description: An interferometer of 42 antennas, each 6 m across, observing about 1-14 GHz for both astronomy and a simultaneous search for extraterrestrial intelligence.
highlights: First light on 11 October 2007 with 42 antennas; 350 dishes were originally planned.
The SETI Institute describes it as the first radio telescope designed specifically for SETI research.
It was funded by Paul Allen and the Paul G. Allen Family Foundation; operations paused between April and August 2011 for lack of funds.

observatories.name: Big Ear radio telescope (Ohio State University Radio Observatory)
observatories.description: A Kraus-type radio telescope operated by Ohio State University for nearly 40 years; it ceased operation in late 1997 and was destroyed in early 1998 after the land was sold to developers. The memorial site is run by NAAPO, not by OSU.
highlights: On 15 August 1977 it recorded the Wow! signal, which lasted the full 72-second window; Jerry Ehman noticed it days later.
The signal came from near the globular cluster M55 in Sagittarius.
Held the Guinness record for the longest-running SETI project.
